Samuel, Karl Ellsworth. I am going to be blunt with you, and I am recording nothing, this is between counsel. My board wants out of the Aurora transaction and they have asked me whether the material adverse change clause gets us there. My reading is that it does not. Revenue is down eleven percent, which is bad, but it is not durationally significant and the clause has a carve-out for market-wide conditions. What concerns me more is the disclosure obligation. Under no circumstances should we go to signing without knowing whether the seller was aware of the supplier claim in March. If they were aware and said nothing, that is a different conversation entirely, and the governing law clause points to arbitration in London, which nobody on my board wants. Tell me how you read it.

Samuel, Diane. Karl will push you tomorrow and he will interrupt you, because that is how he negotiates. So decide now what your one sentence is, and decide how you will get back to it after he cuts in. Two things. First, when a point has to land, put the emphasis at the front of the sentence: not only did the seller fail to disclose the claim, but they also renewed the supply contract in April. Never have I seen a carve-out drafted that broadly. It sounds formal because it is formal, and in a call like this formal is what you want. Second, when he interrupts, do not restart and do not apologise. Say if I may just finish this point, and then finish it. One breath, one sentence, then hand the floor back.
